where: Section 2, dpkg -l bullet (and Quiz Q3 answer, Beyond not affected)
problem: dpkg -l is described as listing 'installed packages'. It actually lists every package recorded in the dpkg database, including packages that were removed but still have configuration files left (state rc) and other non-installed states. A student who runs dpkg -l after apt remove nginx will see nginx listed with state rc and may think the remove failed.
fix: dpkg -l lists packages in the dpkg database with their state; state ii means installed and configured, rc means removed with configuration files still on disk. To see only installed packages, filter: dpkg -l | grep '^ii'.

problem: 'It refreshes metadata as part of the run, so a separate refresh step is often unnecessary' is too absolute. dnf reuses cached metadata until it expires (the metadata expiry timer), so a run soon after a previous one may use cached data and still show old versions.
fix: dnf refresh checks metadata automatically, but it reuses the local cache until that cache expires. Force a refresh when you need current data: sudo dnf --refresh update (or sudo dnf clean expire-cache, then update).

problem: The example counts the kernel upgrade as exactly one new package. On real systems a kernel upgrade installs several packages (image, modules, headers) and keeps the old kernel installed, so 13 could be an undercount. The arithmetic is right for the stated data, but students may generalise wrongly.
fix: Add one line: here the kernel is treated as a single package for the count; a real kernel upgrade pulls in several related packages, and apt lists each one in its summary, so count the packages apt reports, not the number of 'things' upgraded.
